claims.text: Observability is how well you can tell what happened inside a running system from the telemetry it sends out, including for questions nobody planned for when the code was written; monitoring watches answers decided in advance.
claims.source_hint: glossary observability; Majors, Fong-Jones, Miranda, Observability Engineering, ch. 1-2 (observability vs monitoring, unknown unknowns)

claims.text: At stage-2 Đơn Hàng's telemetry is log lines (JSON on the console, shipped by Alloy to Loki) and metrics (/metrics scraped by Prometheus); there is no third kind until stage-3.
The Đơn Hàng API dashboard has a panel '5xx responses per second'; it counts failures across all requests and holds no order id.

RequestLoggingMiddleware is registered before ExceptionHandlingMiddleware, so it wraps it: for a failing request the 'unhandled exception' line is written first, then '{Method} {Path} responded {StatusCode} in {ElapsedMs}ms' with 500.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang @ stage-2: DonHang.Api/Program.cs:106-107; ASP.NET Core docs 'Middleware order'

claims.text: With the JSON console formatter, a log call's message-template placeholders become State fields (request line: Method, Path, StatusCode, ElapsedMs; sender's line: NotificationId, OrderId); every line also has EventId, LogLevel, Category, Message.
At stage-2 the JSON log lines carry no scope fields (IncludeScopes is not set and defaults to false), so the request line and the 'unhandled exception' line hold no request id or trace id.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang @ stage-2: DonHang.Api/appsettings.json, docker-compose.yml:132, outputs/stage-2/scripts/devops/json-logs.txt; .NET docs ConsoleFormatterOptions.IncludeScopes

claims.text: ExceptionHandlingMiddleware's last catch (line 61) calls logger.LogError(ex, "unhandled exception") and answers 500; the call passes no method or path, so the line has LogLevel Error, its Category, Message 'unhandled exception' and the exception text.
POST /api/v1/orders for product 999 breaks a foreign key on save, falls to the generic catch and answers 500; loki-query.sh prints '-> 500' and the line 'POST /api/v1/orders responded 500 in ...ms'.
NotificationSender sends an order's email on a later tick of its loop (every 2 s), after the request has answered, and logs 'Sent notification {NotificationId} for order {OrderId}'.

Loki stores each line with a timestamp (the api's JSON lines carry none of their own); a LogQL line filter |= keeps lines containing the string, and | json turns the line's JSON properties into labels.
claims.source_hint: Grafana Loki docs: LogQL log queries (line filter expressions, json parser)

claims.text: At stage-3 one refund passes through DonHang.Api, RabbitMQ, DonHang.Payments and DonHang.Notifications, each a separate process writing its own log lines.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang @ stage-3: STAGE.md; docker-compose.yml (services api, payments, notifications, rabbitmq)

claims.text: Opinion: linking log lines by time works only while requests do not overlap; with concurrent requests and more services, matching by time becomes a guess.
claims.source_hint: Observability Engineering, ch. 6-7 (why correlating by timestamp fails in distributed systems)

claims.text: Grafana's Explore view lets you choose the Loki data source and switch the query editor from Builder to Code to type LogQL as text.
claims.source_hint: content devops.l2.centralized-logs Try it (verified); Grafana docs 'Explore' / Loki query editor
